data.body:
ROUND 3: BLOCK, two findings, both ACCEPTED. Neither is a nitpick and the second is my own
inconsistency introduced while fixing the first.

FINDING 1 — AC2 said the in-process blindness must be "recorded as evidence" and never named the
ARTIFACT. Fair: "recorded" with no location is unverifiable, and a completion verifier reading
repository files cannot confirm a claim that lives nowhere. Now specified concretely as two
artifacts: (a) the new test module's DOCSTRING must state that an in-process assertion stays green
when the workflow_ops.py:45 import is deleted and why the subprocess form is therefore mandatory —
that is the copy a future reader hits before "simplifying" it away; (b) a COMMENT ON THIS TICKET
quoting both observed outputs, the subprocess run reporting the missing op and the in-process run
passing, so the contrast is checkable rather than asserted.

FINDING 2 — AC3 HAD THE IDENTICAL DEFECT AND I LEFT IT. When I remediated AC1 to require subprocess
isolation, I did not carry the same requirement to AC3, even though the gate-YAML resolution test
reads the SAME process-global STEP_REGISTRY (executor.py:155). A pre-populated registry makes that
assertion pass regardless of whether the registration imports survive, so it too would be blind to
the defect it exists to catch. Fixed: AC3 now requires the same subprocess isolation and says
explicitly that sharing one helper between the two checks is preferred.

THE PATTERN WORTH NAMING, because it is the third instance on this ticket: each round I fixed the
specific thing the reviewer cited and did not sweep for OTHER instances of the same class. Round 2's
finding was "this assertion depends on a process-global pre-populated by imports"; the correct
response was to ask which OTHER assertions in the plan share that dependency, and AC3 obviously did.
Rather than wait for a round 4 to tell me, I swept the remaining criteria myself: AC4 is a pure LOC
read, AC5 is a text correction, AC6 is a no-op statement — none touches process-global state, so the
class is now fully covered by AC1-AC3.

Round 1 was a factual error (a docstring I called stale that was accurate). Round 2 was an
unexecutable falsification claim. Round 3 is an under-specified artifact plus a missed sibling. The
findings are getting narrower each round, which is convergence rather than thrash — but all three
share one cause: asserting something without running or sweeping for it.
